blocks.content: While the CBI requires state consent to investigate cases within a state, the NIA possesses statutory concurrent jurisdiction across India to investigate terror-related scheduled offenses without state permission.

rows: Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions (DoPT)
Corruption, Economic Offenses, and Special Crimes

items: CBI is NOT a statutory body; it was created by an executive resolution of the Ministry of Home Affairs in 1963.
NIA IS a statutory body created by the NIA Act, 2008.
CBI requires state consent (General or Specific) to investigate in a state, unless directed by the High Court or Supreme Court.
NIA does NOT require state consent to register and investigate scheduled offenses anywhere in India.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: CBI operates under the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT), whereas NIA functions under the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA).
CBI derives its investigative powers from the Delhi Special Police Establishment (DSPE) Act, 1946, and is not a statutory body.
NIA is a statutory body constituted under the National Investigation Agency Act, 2008, following the 26/11 Mumbai terror attacks.
CBI requires state consent to investigate crimes within state territory, whereas NIA has statutory concurrent jurisdiction nationwide for scheduled offenses.
CBI primarily deals with corruption, economic crimes, and complex special crimes, while NIA focuses specifically on counter-terrorism and national security offenses.
